key_finding: A field experiment nudge shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field RCT on credit cardholders with six-month follow-up on autopay enrollment, payment amounts, and debt.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise in a comparable consumer financial product: shifting enrollment behavior did not change the underlying financial outcome, warning that our enrollment lift may not translate into more savings.
limitations: studies credit card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
does not test preset multiplier anchoring directly
relevance_reason: Field RCT on consumer financial defaults showing enrollment change without behavioral improvement, directly informing the entry-mechanism and 'vanity metric' concern.

key_finding: Abstract-only synthesis: reviews how automatic enrollment and default investment options affect participation short- and long-term, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: abstract-only narrative overview of defined-contribution plan design literature.
why_it_matters: Summarizes the engagement costs of passive enrollment across the closest analogous literature, giving context on disengagement risk, though the employer-trust mechanism it relies on does not carry over to a consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
abstract gives no explicit effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent comprehensive review of default/enrollment effects in the closest analogous (employer) literature, useful as synthesis context.

key_finding: Abstract-only: argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces passivity — low contribution rates, disengagement, account churn — undermining long-term welfare gains unless paired with escalation and re-enrollment mechanisms.
methodology: abstract-only narrative/policy discussion citing broader empirical literature on default enrollment.
why_it_matters: Explicitly voices the support team's disengagement concern about passively-enrolled users and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) relevant to the level-setting decision.
limitations: employer retirement plan framing
perspective piece with no original data or effect sizes
relevance_reason: States the 'passive trap' critique of default enrollment that mirrors the brief's internal disagreement almost verbatim.

key_finding: Abstract-only: proposes a taxonomy and framework explaining when default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: abstract-only theoretical synthesis and taxonomy of consumer default-effect literature, with a proposed research agenda.
why_it_matters: Gives a conceptual map of exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief raises and flags which factors (antecedent preferences, salience) predict whether enrolled-by-default users will disengage from the round-up feature.
limitations: theoretical taxonomy rather than an empirical estimate
no financial-product-specific data
relevance_reason: Recent consumer-behavior framework directly targeting when and why default effects persist or decay over time, matching the brief's persistence question.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even to substantial losses from the default option.
methodology: Three natural/randomized experiments using random assignment to default options among Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows default stickiness can persist even when it hurts the enrollee, cautioning against assuming an opt-out default is automatically welfare-improving for disengaged consumers.
limitations: health insurance/drug benefit setting, not a financial savings product
low-income Medicare population differs from a general banking app user base
relevance_reason: Strong evidence on persistence and insensitivity of passive default behavior, with distributional detail on low-income beneficiaries, relevant by analogy to sticky opt-out defaults.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine automatic enrollment and auto-escalation effects: steady-state savings rates rise only 0.6% and 0.3% of income respectively, and only 40% of employees complete their first auto-escalation before opting out.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job turnover, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out over the medium/long run.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: the enrollment lift from defaults shrinks sharply once turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for, directly bearing on whether our enrollment numbers will be vanity.
limitations: 401(k) retirement accounts, not liquid consumer round-up savings
employer-plan turnover dynamics don't map onto an app-based product
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies how much smaller default effects are over the medium/long run than initial estimates suggest, matching the brief's core persistence question.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most low-income individuals actively opted out, with the default effect stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrollment status was lacking.
methodology: Natural policy experiment using linked administrative and survey data on nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees.
why_it_matters: Shows default enrollment gains can be substantially eroded by active opt-out and depend heavily on incentive salience and awareness, cautioning against assuming a stable, uniform enrollment lift.
limitations: public pension system, not a consumer banking app
low-income employee population differs from typical fintech users
relevance_reason: Quantified default effect with heterogeneity by knowledge/incentive and majority opt-out, informing the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains in participation and contributions attenuate substantially between 12 months and 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a UK panel, combined with a life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question: the enrollment/savings lift from defaults measured at signup does not hold up over 1-3 years, cautioning against reading initial enrollment numbers as durable.
limitations: retirement savings plans, not liquid consumer savings
life-cycle model calibrated to pension behavior
relevance_reason: Quantifies exactly how much default effects on savings shrink between 12 and 36 months, the timeframe the brief asks about.

key_finding: Default nudges have medium-to-large effects on consumer risk-taking, but a default nudge (especially one people refuse) lowers ratings of the wealth manager's honesty and advice quality, with framing of the ask also shifting invested amounts.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative five-European-country sample (n=4207), on default-nudged financial investment decisions.
why_it_matters: Provides EU consumer evidence that defaults can damage trust and perceived honesty — central to the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry-mechanism decision — and shows framing of the contribution ask shifts amounts, relevant to how the multiplier field is worded.
limitations: financial-advisor context rather than a self-serve app
risk-taking investment decisions, not round-up savings specifically
relevance_reason: Directly measures manipulation perception and framing effects of defaults among EU consumers in a financial-advice context, matching the brief's dark-pattern and framing concerns.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants anchored on the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative data analysis across three large firms tracking 401(k) participation and default anchoring over three years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level strongly anchors the chosen contribution amount for years — the foundational evidence behind the brief's anchoring concern for the round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
old, foundational study predating current fintech/regulatory context
relevance_reason: Foundational study establishing that preset default levels anchor participant choices persistently, the classic evidence the anchoring literature builds on.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together, and a counterfactual added preset (15% alongside 20/25/30) captures 69% of achievable welfare gains at 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on NYC taxi transaction data plus a stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu simulations.
why_it_matters: The deviation-cost/opt-out-cost decomposition and counterfactual preset-menu method is the specific technique for deciding which round-up multiplier value to pre-select and how many preset options to offer, transferring directly to the level-design decision.
limitations: taxi tipping, not financial savings
no data on longer-term persistence of chosen behavior
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: its structural friction-decomposition and counterfactual preset-menu analysis is directly applicable to choosing and testing which multiplier to pre-select.

key_finding: Opt-in take-up of a payroll-deduction short-term liquid savings account was under 0.7% of eligible employees, but among activators, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a short-term (liquid) savings program rollout across five UK firms, tracking activation and 12-month usage.
why_it_matters: The closest available product analog (liquid, opt-in short-term savings) shows opt-in enrollment is very low but engaged users persist strongly — directly informative for weighing the entry-mechanism trade-off even though it lacks an opt-out/active-choice comparison arm.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction context rather than a standalone consumer app
opt-in only, no opt-out or active-choice comparison arm
relevance_reason: Closest liquid, opt-in short-term savings analog with 12-month persistence data directly relevant to the entry decision, despite being employer-mediated.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, passive automatic employer contributions raised savings substantially while active-choice tax subsidies mostly shifted assets between accounts (1 cent of new saving per $1 of subsidy); ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by automatic defaults, while active savers are wealthier and more sophisticated.
methodology: Population-level administrative panel data from Denmark comparing responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive automatic contributions.
why_it_matters: The classic evidence that passive defaults reach financially unsophisticated savers that active-choice policies miss — central to the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question when weighing active choice against opt-out.
limitations: Danish retirement/taxable savings accounts, not a consumer app
outside the recency window the brief prioritizes
relevance_reason: Foundational distributional evidence on who benefits from passive defaults versus active-choice policies, directly relevant to the brief's equity concern.

key_finding: Proposes and tests 'enhanced active choice' — a variant of active choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrollment when defaults are infeasible or unethical, via field experiments in medication adherence.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against standard framing; abstract-only, health-care/medication-adherence context.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the active-choice option for the entry decision: shows active choice can be strengthened by loss-framing rather than treated as a weaker compromise between opt-in and opt-out, which matters if the team wants active choice to capture more of the opt-out enrolment lift.
limitations: setting is medication adherence, not consumer financial products
no effect sizes for savings-specific behavior
field experiments are in health care, not fintech
relevance_reason: One of the foundational papers introducing and testing active choice as a named alternative to opt-in/opt-out defaults, directly bearing on the entry-mechanism decision even though the domain differs.

key_finding: A broad review of household financial behavior and behavioral-economics explanations for it, covering consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, plus a survey of interventions (education, peer effects, product design, advice/disclosure, choice architecture, and price/quantity mandates) firms and governments use to shape those behaviors.
methodology: Narrative literature-review chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and behavioral models across household finance; abstract-only, no primary data or effect sizes given.
why_it_matters: Gives the broader theoretical backdrop for why choice-architecture interventions (defaults, product design) are expected to work in consumer financial contexts, useful for framing but not for sizing either the entry or level decision.
limitations: no quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract
covers many domains at a survey level rather than round-up savings specifically
may lean heavily on employer-retirement literature within its household-finance framing
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of behavioral household finance and choice-architecture interventions, useful as background context on the mechanisms the brief invokes, though not specific enough to move either design decision on its own.
